notes.title: 잃어버리다 vs 잊어버리다
notes.text: They sound alike but are different: 잃어버리다 = to lose a thing (열쇠를 잃어버렸어요), 잊어버리다 = to forget (이름을 잊어버렸어요). -아/어 버리다 adds a feeling of "completely, and it's too late."

notes.title: -는데
notes.text: -는데 sets up background before your main point: 비가 오는데 우산 있어요? ("It's raining — do you have an umbrella?"). Ending a sentence with -는데요 politely leaves something unsaid, very common on the phone.

notes.title: Three levels of speech
notes.text: Polite 해요체 (-어요) is what you've learned — safe with almost anyone. Formal 합니다체 (-습니다) is for news, speeches, announcements, the military and customer service. Casual 반말 (-어) is for close friends, kids and family. You'll learn 반말 in Phase 2.

notes.title: Peeling an apple
notes.text: In Korea, peeling and cutting fruit for someone is a quiet way of saying "I care about you" — or "I'm sorry." Watch for it in dramas.

notes.title: Phase 1 complete!
notes.text: You've reached the end of Phase 1: the ~1,000 core words of Korean, polite speech, and the most important grammar. In Phase 2, the housemates start speaking casually (반말) with you — and the mystery of the key begins.
